comparability.reason: Bench-scale BN-assisted ball milling of undiluted AFFF represents a specialized mechanochemical system with piezoelectric BN and undiluted foam matrix; endpoints emphasize nearly complete inorganic fluoride release relative to TOF and disappearance of many precursors, which are not directly comparable to most aqueous-phase PFAS treatment studies focused on parent removal without fluorine-balance closure.

endpoints.interpretation: Loss of parent surfactant precursors (6:2 FTS, 8:2 FTS, and other n = 6–7 precursors) and disappearance of PFCA intermediates (PFHxA, PFOA) in undiluted AFFF during BN-BM treatment, as determined by targeted LC-MS and Q-ToF-HRMS; authors describe this as destruction of targeted PFAS and precursors after 6 h.
endpoints.reported_term: PFAS destruction efficiency; destruction of FTS and precursors; decay of PFAS concentrations

endpoints.interpretation: Release of inorganic fluoride from organic fluorine in AFFF, quantified as defluorination efficiency DeF(%) based on measured F− yield relative to initial TOF. Reported 99.7% defluorination of undiluted AFFF after 6 h; authors interpret near-complete defluorination as evidence for PFAS mineralization and mitigated risk, but only F− and TOF were directly measured.
endpoints.reported_term: defluorination efficiency (DeF); near-complete defluorination; bulk defluorination of AFFF

endpoints.interpretation: Change in total organofluorine pool of AFFF inferred from comparison of F− production with initial TOF; fluorine balance data used to calculate DeF and assess near-complete defluorination of the complex AFFF mixture.

Authors state that near-complete defluorination of individual [SOURCE_TEXT_OMITTED sha256=fde074c762d0e44516df9c0a9e9cd33671dbe9515661d8752aedc1507c148e54]; however, no direct mineralization metrics (e.g., CO2, inorganic carbon) are reported, so mineralization is inferred rather than analytically demonstrated.

limitations.statement: Near-complete defluorination is used as a proxy for PFAS mineralization and risk mitigation, but no direct carbon mineralization metrics (e.g., CO2 evolution) are reported.
Fluorine balance and defluorination calculations rely on extraction of PFAS and fluoride into selected solvents (e.g., 50% MeOH), which may leave unextractable fluorinated species unaccounted for.

comparability.reason: The tandem evaporation plus BN+SiO2-BM process treats large-volume undiluted AFFF in a mechanochemical regime where both PFAS destruction and fluoride immobilization on solids occur; multiple coupled endpoints (parent PFAS loss, partial defluorination, TOC remaining, and immobilized fluoride) complicate direct comparison with other PFAS treatments that focus solely on aqueous-phase parent removal or do not quantify fluorine and carbon balances.

endpoints.interpretation: Destruction of target PFAS measured by decrease in concentrations of selected AFFF PFAS after the tandem evaporation plus BN+SiO2-BM treatment of 1000 µL AFFF; more than 90% destruction reported.

Defluorination efficiency quantified by inorganic fluoride yield relative to initial TOF for AFFF. For 1000 µL AFFF with evaporation pretreatment and BN+SiO2-BM, DeF exceeded 60%, interpreted as significant but lower than for BN-only treatments of smaller volumes, in part because SiO2 may immobilize a portion of released fluoride.

Fluorine balance for AFFF combining TOF and fluoride measurements used to calculate DeF for the large-volume tandem treatment; incomplete DeF indicates a remaining organofluorine fraction or immobilized fluoride on solids.

Approximately 50% of the total organic carbon (TOC) of AFFF remained after BN-BM treatment, indicating substantial but incomplete removal of organic carbon; this is an indirect mineralization-related endpoint but does not demonstrate full mineralization.
endpoints.reported_term: total organic carbon (TOC) remaining after BN-BM treatment

limitations.statement: Defluorination efficiency for the tandem evaporation + BN+SiO2-BM treatment (~>60%) is lower than the near-complete defluorination achieved in BN-only systems, likely due in part to immobilization of fluoride on SiO2 surfaces and incomplete liberation of fluorine from all PFAS or their byproducts.
TOC measurements indicate that about half of the organic carbon remains after BN-BM treatment, demonstrating that near-complete defluorination does not equate to full carbon mineralization.

Z (effective liquid film thickness) is used as a theoretical descriptor of collision environment and not directly measured; assumptions about wetting (e.g., hydrophobic BN surface) mean Z is an estimate and may not precisely represent local films surrounding PFAS-containing liquids during milling.

record.citation: Pinkard, B.R.; Shetty, S.; Stritzinger, D.; Bellona, C.; Novosselov, I.V. Destruction of perfluorooctanesulfonate (PFOS) in a batch supercritical water oxidation reactor. Chemosphere 2021, 279, 130834.

comparability.reason: The study reports PFOS parent loss ("destruction"/conversion) and defluorination efficiencies as percentages under well-specified SCWO operating conditions (temperature, residence time, pressure). These endpoints and denominators (initial PFOS and total fluorine) are standard for PFAS treatment performance and, with attention to batch SCWO configuration and aqueous feed, can be compared conditionally with other PFAS destruction studies using similar percentage-based metrics.

endpoints.interpretation: Loss of PFOS parent compound in the liquid phase was quantified and reported as percent destruction/conversion versus temperature and residence time, with maximum 70.0% PFOS destruction at 500 °C after 60 min.
endpoints.reported_term: PFOS destruction, PFOS conversion, extent of destruction

endpoints.interpretation: Inorganic fluoride production from PFOS was measured and expressed as defluorination efficiency (percent fluorine conversion), with a maximum of 78.2% at 500 °C after 60 min; fluorine mass balance across reagents and products was also evaluated.
endpoints.reported_term: defluorination efficiency, fluoride production, fluorine conversion

endpoints.interpretation: Total fluorine recovery was calculated as a mass balance from initial PFOS to measured fluoride and organofluorine species. Mass balance was >75% at 475 and 500 °C, but not well closed at 425 and 450 °C, indicating an unidentified organofluorine fraction, likely including gaseous fluorinated species.
endpoints.reported_term: total fluorine mass balance, fluorine mass balance from reagents to products

endpoints.interpretation: Targeted LC-QToF-MS analysis of liquid products did not indicate production of intermediate fluorocarbons such as additional perfluoroalkane sulfonates, perfluoroalkanoic acids, or fluorotelomer sulfonates/alkanoic acids beyond PFOS, PFHpS, and PFHxS (in decreasing levels), implying either rapid further transformation or formation of undetected lower-molecular-weight fluorinated species, especially at lower temperatures where fluorine mass balance was poor.

Authors use the term 'destruction' to describe PFOS conversion and defluorination in SCWO, but direct mineralization endpoints (e.g., CO2 production, carbon balance) were not reported, so 'destruction' corresponds primarily to parent loss and defluorination rather than confirmed full mineralization.
endpoints.reported_term: destruction efficiency, efficacy for PFAS destruction

limitations.statement: Gaseous products were not analyzed; authors cite difficulty of performing non-targeted analysis of fluorocarbons in the gaseous phase at low concentrations via GC-MS, which limits identification of volatile fluorinated byproducts and contributes to poor fluorine mass balance at lower temperatures.

Fluorine mass balance was not well closed for experiments at 425 and 450 °C, suggesting formation of lower molecular weight fluorinated species in gaseous and/or liquid phases that were not captured in targeted analyses.

Transformation products were assessed only by targeted LC-QToF-MS for a defined set of perfluoroalkane sulfonates, perfluoroalkanoic acids, and fluorotelomer species, so unidentified organofluorine intermediates could remain undetected.

Experiments were conducted in a bench-scale batch SCWO reactor on PFOS-containing feed under specific temperature (425-500 °C), pressure (~25 MPa), and residence time (0-60 min) conditions, which may limit direct extrapolation to other PFAS, matrices, or continuous-flow systems.

comparability.reason: Bench-scale continuous-flow SCWO treating concentrated aqueous PFAS mixtures, with LC-MS/MS for parent PFAS and IC for fluoride, across a defined temperature range (510–650 °C). Endpoints (DRE, LC-MS/MS non-detects, and fluoride production) are directly comparable across temperatures within this study when accounting for slightly varying influent PFAS concentrations.

endpoints.interpretation: Parent PFAS concentrations in liquid effluent were measured by LC-MS/MS to compute DRE. At 510 °C, all PFCAs in the mixture were below the method detection limit, while PFSAs (PFOS and PFHpS) showed DRE <40%, indicating incomplete destruction of sulfonates at this temperature.

Defluorination was assessed by measuring inorganic fluoride in the effluent via ion chromatography and comparing to the initial fluorine content (sum of F atoms in PFAS in the stock). In the 510–610 °C range, defluorination lagged behind parent PFAS destruction, suggesting formation of fluorinated intermediates; at 510 °C, fluoride levels were increased relative to untreated but did not indicate complete defluorination.

Initial fluorine was computed from the F atoms in all detected PFAS in the stock solution. After SCWO, HF formed in the reactor was neutralized to NaF during sampling and quantified by ion chromatography to estimate conversion of organic-bound fluorine to inorganic fluoride; no full fluorine balance closure is explicitly reported in the available text.

limitations.statement: Defluorination and identification of intermediates were limited by a lack of analysis of gaseous and liquid-phase byproducts, and the authors note that generalized fluorine transformation routes cannot be established without more comprehensive intermediate and gas-phase measurements.

Kinetic rates and detailed reaction pathways for PFAS destruction in SCWO were not established; the authors highlight the need for in-depth kinetic studies to optimize SCWO reactors for practical PFAS waste treatment.
The mixture of PFSA and PFCA complicates attribution of any observed intermediates to specific parent compounds, making degradation routes for individual PFAS in mixtures difficult to resolve.

comparability.reason: This high-temperature (650 °C) condition represents the upper bound of a controlled temperature series in the same bench-scale continuous-flow SCWO system treating the same PFAS aqueous matrix, with consistent analytical methods (LC-MS/MS for parent PFAS and IC for fluoride). DRE and defluorination efficiencies are directly comparable across the study’s temperature range when accounting for residence time and influent concentration variations.

endpoints.interpretation: Parent PFAS concentrations in the liquid effluent were quantified by LC-MS/MS to calculate DRE. At 650 °C and ~30 s residence time, DRE exceeded 99.999%, and only trace PFOS at 1.66 µg/L was detected among targeted PFAS, indicating near-complete loss of parent PFAS from the liquid phase.

Inorganic fluoride in the liquid effluent was measured by ion chromatography after neutralization of HF to NaF, and compared with initial organic-bound fluorine. At 650 °C and 30 s, the authors report complete defluorination with fluoride recovery consistent with conversion of PFAS-bound fluorine to dissolved fluoride, though detailed fluorine mass-balance closure values are not provided in the available text.

The initial fluorine concentration was calculated as the sum of F atoms in each PFAS detected in the stock solution. Post-treatment fluoride was measured as dissolved NaF by ion chromatography. This mass-balance approach distinguishes between parent PFAS removal and conversion of organofluorine to inorganic fluoride, but does not, in the reported text, track carbon products (no mineralization endpoint) or fully resolve unidentified fluorine fractions.

limitations.statement: The study does not report direct measurements of CO2 or other carbon-species balances, so mineralization and overall carbon fate of PFAS cannot be fully assessed from the available endpoints.

Gas-phase fluorinated organic byproducts and volatile organofluorines were not comprehensively analyzed in this experiments series, and the authors note that failure to identify and capture potentially harmful liquid and gaseous byproducts can have environmental and health implications.

The authors emphasize that existing data, including this work, are insufficient to propose generalized fluorine transformation routes in SCWO due to limited analysis of intermediates in both gas and liquid phases.

comparability.reason: The available excerpts provide treatment conditions, analytical framework, and feed composition, but do not report specific numerical values for PFAS percent degradation, defluorination, or F mass recovery for individual runs. Without these quantitative performance metrics, the record mainly informs measurement requirements and conceptual endpoints rather than providing directly comparable destruction efficiencies.

endpoints.interpretation: Loss of target PFAS concentration (total and by subclass) measured by LC-MS/MS and expressed as %Degradation using C0 and C (Eq. 1). This tracks disappearance of monitored PFAS analytes but does not by itself demonstrate destruction or defluorination.

Defluorination defined and calculated as conversion of organofluorine to inorganic fluoride using Eq. (2). The authors use terms quantitative defluorination and mineralization interchangeably for organofluorine-to-inorganic-fluoride conversion, but this endpoint specifically reflects fluorine speciation (IF vs TOF) rather than full carbon mineralization.

Fluorine mass balance calculated as %F mass recovery from inorganic fluoride (IF) plus total organic fluorine (TOF) relative to initial IF+TOF (Eq. 3). TOF and IF were measured to assess closure of fluorine mass balance and to infer the presence or absence of unidentified organofluorine species.

endpoints.interpretation: Formation of volatile organofluorine species measured in the gas phase by in-line FTIR and GC-MS, with normalized [VOF] values reported as a function of operating conditions (temperature, NaOH concentration, flow). This endpoint captures partitioning to gas and formation of volatile byproducts rather than destruction.

limitations.statement: Few pilot demonstrations of HALT have been performed to date and HALT had not yet been permanently implemented in industrial wastewater applications at the time of the study.

Defluorination is defined as conversion of organofluorine to inorganic fluoride, and is sometimes termed mineralization by the authors; however, no direct carbon mineralization measurements (e.g., CO2) are reported in the provided excerpts, so full mineralization cannot be confirmed from the described endpoints alone.
Some species in the feed streams were consistently below method detection limits as noted in supplementary information, indicating potential analytical censoring for low-level constituents.

record.citation: Kumar, A.; Georgi, A.; Huaccallo-Aguilar, Y.; Meier, M.; Kryk, H.; Reinecke, S.F.; Hampel, U. Degradation and defluorination of perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) forever chemical in water using hydrodynamic cavitation treatment. Chemical Engineering Journal Advances 2026, 25, 101046.

comparability.reason: Study reports PFOS degradation, defluorination, and fluorine mass balance in a defined aqueous matrix using a single orifice-based hydrodynamic cavitation system at specified initial concentration (5 mg/L), with quantified detection limits for parent PFAS, fluoride, and key transformation products. Endpoints (parent loss, F− release, total fluorine balance, inferred mineralization) are clearly defined, making the record comparable to other bench-scale aqueous PFAS destruction studies under similar concentration ranges and with fluorine mass-balance measurements, provided that differences in matrix, PFAS identity, and endpoint definitions are accounted for.

endpoints.interpretation: Loss of parent PFOS in aqueous phase measured by HPLC–MS and interpreted as degradation; degradation per pass up to ~1.6% reported. Parent loss is taken by authors as evidence of molecular breakdown but, by itself, does not confirm mineralization or complete destruction.
endpoints.reported_term: PFOS degradation; PFOS degradation ratios; PFOS removal

endpoints.interpretation: Release of inorganic fluoride (F−) to the aqueous phase from PFOS and decrease of organically bound fluorine in parent PFOS were used to calculate defluorination percentage over time, reaching ~20% by the end of treatment at 5 mg/L. Authors interpret this as defluorination accompanying PFOS degradation.

Total fluorine (TF) was evaluated as the sum of measured inorganic fluoride and fluorine calculated from residual PFOS. Mass balance closure of 97–104% over the treatment time supports conservation of fluorine and enables distinguishing fluorine released as F− from fluorine remaining in organic form.
endpoints.reported_term: Fluorine mass balance; F− recovery; total fluorine

endpoints.interpretation: Mineralization is inferred (not directly measured via CO2) from high fluoride yield relative to degraded PFOS, absence of shorter-chain perfluorocarboxylates above a 0.05 mol% detection limit in the aqueous phase, and near-complete fluorine mass balance. Authors state that PFOS reaching the cavitation bubble undergoes near-complete mineralization to CO2 and F−, but this is based on indirect evidence (F− release and lack of detectable intermediates), not on direct carbon fate measurements.
endpoints.reported_term: Mineralization; near-complete mineralization; PFOS mineralization into CO2 and F−

endpoints.interpretation: Shorter-chain perfluorocarboxylates in the aqueous phase were monitored by LC–MS as potential transformation products and were not detected above 0.05 mol% of the initial PFOS. Authors note that some deviation in fluoride mass balance in early stages may be due in part to formation of stable fluorinated intermediates (potentially non-aqueous phase or undetected), but the main observation is the absence of detectable chain-shortened perfluorocarboxylates in solution under the conditions tested.
endpoints.reported_term: Formation of stable fluorinated intermediates; transformation by-products; chain-shortened intermediates

limitations.statement: Results at lower initial PFOS concentrations were subject to greater uncertainty, likely due to sorption losses and interfacial effects, complicating quantitative interpretation; experiments at 5 mg/L provided more consistent and reliable results for degradation/defluorination and fluoride mass balance.

The proposed near-complete mineralization mechanism is not definitively proven because direct carbon-fate measurements (e.g., CO2 quantification) were not reported; mineralization is inferred from fluoride release, fluorine mass balance, and lack of detected shorter-chain intermediates.

record.citation: Juriasingani, P.; Arnseth, R.; Davis, J.; Meegoda, J. Field Demonstration of a High-Frequency Ultrasonic Treatment Reactor for [PFAS-Contaminated Groundwater]. Groundwater Monitoring & Remediation, 2026, doi:10.1111/gwmr.70045.

comparability.reason: The study is a field demonstration in a site-specific groundwater matrix using a proprietary high-frequency ultrasonic reactor, with variable treatment times and grouped PFAS metrics (e.g., long-chain PFAS, top six PFAS) and a simplified fluorine mass balance. Parent loss, AOF change, and fluoride production are all measured but with only one influent fluorine characterization and incomplete analyte coverage (no ultrashort PFAS). These conditions and endpoints are valuable mechanistically but are not directly comparable on a quantitative basis to controlled bench-scale destruction studies or to treatments in different matrices without substantial normalization and additional data.

endpoints.interpretation: Decrease in concentration of individual and grouped parent PFAS (e.g., PFOA, PFOS, long-chain PFAS, 4:2 FTS, 6:2 FTS) between influent and effluent or across treatment time, expressed as degradation efficiency. This measures parent-compound loss and removal in the treated groundwater, which the authors interpret as PFAS destruction.
Increase in aqueous fluoride concentration as PFAS concentrations and AOF decreased was used to infer that a portion of PFAS organic fluorine was mineralized to inorganic fluoride (defluorination).
endpoints.reported_term: Mineralization of PFAS-bound fluorine to fluoride

endpoints.interpretation: AOF was measured in influent and effluent and compared (in moles of fluorine) to six dominant PFAS and to fluoride to establish an organic-fluorine mass balance. The total decrease in AOF-defined organofluorine exceeded the increase in fluoride, indicating incomplete closure of the fluorine mass balance and suggesting transformation to other unmeasured organofluorine species or analytical gaps (e.g., ultrashort PFAS).
endpoints.reported_term: Decrease in adsorbable organic fluorine (AOF) and PFAS-bound fluorine

endpoints.interpretation: The authors describe high-frequency ultrasound as mineralizing PFAS to fluoride and CO2 based on prior bench-scale work. In this field study, mineralization is inferred from partial conversion of AOF to fluoride, but complete carbon mineralization (e.g., CO2 measurement) was not reported in the provided text, so mineralization evidence is limited to fluorine-side mass balance rather than full carbon fate.

A simplified fluorine mass balance was conducted using three measures: (1) sum of fluorine in six PFAS with highest concentrations, (2) AOF, and (3) total fluoride. These were converted to moles of fluorine and compared between influent and effluent to estimate the fraction of PFAS-bound fluorine converted to fluoride and to evaluate creation of shorter-chain PFAS not otherwise quantified.

limitations.statement: Fluoride and AOF were analyzed in only one chamber per reactor and only a single influent characterization sample was collected before tests, limiting the precision of fluorine mass balance and temporal resolution of mineralization assessment.

Ultrashort PFAS such as TFA were not evaluated due to exclusion from current USEPA analytical methods, so production of TFA or other ultrashort-chain PFAS as transformation products could not be confirmed or ruled out, contributing to incomplete fluorine mass balance.

Treatment duration was the only primary variable changed among tests, and key reactor operating parameters (e.g., specific frequency, power density) were not reported in the provided text, limiting transferability of performance metrics.

comparability.reason: The study evaluates a single field-scale continuous-flow SCWO system treating a specific concentrated AFFF-derived PFAS waste under particular operating conditions, with partial fluorine mass balance (liquid fluoride only) and a limited transformation-product scope (12 PFAAs plus observation of short-chain changes). These constraints and the incomplete fluorine accounting make the quantitative DRE%, defluorination ratio, and EEM suitable as detailed case-study descriptors but not directly comparable without adjustment to other technologies or studies that use different PFAS suites, matrices, or more complete destruction/mineralization endpoints.

endpoints.interpretation: DRE% was calculated for the sum of 12 target PFAAs based on influent versus liquid and gaseous effluent PFAA mass flows, yielding >99.999% reduction after two ~120-min continuous-flow SCWO trials. This endpoint reflects near-complete loss of the targeted parent PFAAs but does not by itself distinguish between transformation to other organic fluorinated products and full mineralization.

A theoretical organic fluorine loading in the influent AFFF was calculated from quantified PFAAs and compared to measured inorganic fluoride in the liquid effluent to estimate an overall defluorination ratio of ~62.6%. A partial fluorine mole balance indicated that about 28.1% of the expected fluorine (152.9 mmol) was not recovered in measured fluoride, implying an unidentified fluorine-containing fraction (e.g., unmeasured organofluorine species or unmeasured phases such as gas). Gaseous fluoride was not measured, so the defluorination assessment is incomplete.
endpoints.reported_term: overall defluorination ratio; fluorine mole balance

endpoints.interpretation: PFAA mass in the gaseous effluent (stack) was quantified via OTM-45 sampling. The gaseous PFAA mass was on average 42 µg, corresponding to 0.0003% of the measured influent PFAA mass, demonstrating that only a negligible fraction of parent PFAAs were transferred to the gas phase under the tested SCWO conditions.

An energy efficiency metric (EEM) of 1.1×10^5 kW·h/kg PFAS was calculated for the SCWO system under the tested conditions, representing electrical energy consumption per unit mass of PFAS treated. This is an operational performance endpoint rather than a direct chemical fate measure.

An increase of 3.8%–50.8% in the sum of short-chain PFAAs (ΣPFAA SC) was observed in some cases. The authors state that the available data do not allow them to distinguish whether this increase reflects incomplete mineralization of fluorotelomer- or precursor-like species (ΣPFAALC) or comparatively less effective SCWO of sulfonamide/sulfonate-like short-chain species (ΣPFAASC), indicating formation or persistence of certain transformation products even as long-chain target PFAAs are largely removed.

limitations.statement: Gaseous fluoride (in steam) was not measured due to budget and time constraints, so the fluorine mass balance and defluorination ratio are incomplete and based only on liquid-phase fluoride.

The available data do not allow a definitive conclusion about whether the observed 3.8%–50.8% increase in short-chain PFAAs (ΣPFAA SC) is due to incomplete mineralization of precursor-like species (ΣPFAALC) or comparatively less effective SCWO of certain short-chain sulfonate/sulfonamide PFAAs (ΣPFAASC).

Fluorine mass balance is partial: approximately 28.1% (152.9 mmol) of anticipated fluorine was not recovered, implying unmeasured fluorine-containing phases or species and limiting conclusions about complete destruction versus transformation.
Gaseous PFAAs were only quantified for the parent suite covered by OTM-45; transformation products not targeted by the method could exist in the gas phase but were not assessed.

endpoints.reported_term: destructive treatment; advanced treatment method for removal of hazardous pollutants

limitations.statement: Formation of transformation products (including PFAS and other halogenated compounds) is a known and unwanted issue during EO and other advanced oxidation processes, and this study emphasizes that more research is needed to determine the concentrations and toxicity of such products, as well as potential emissions of unknown transformation products to air.

Most previous EO studies have relied on targeted quantification of known PFAS using triple-quadrupole mass spectrometry, providing limited insight into unknown transformation products; this motivates the use of suspect and non-target screening and is presented as a knowledge gap for PFAS-destructive treatments.

The water matrix (landfill leachate vs groundwater and their co-contaminant profiles) plays an important role in the types of transformation products that can form during EO, complicating generalization of results across matrices and indicating a need for matrix-specific studies.

This study does not report comprehensive mass-balance closure or direct mineralization measurements (e.g., CO2 or total fluorine balances), limiting its ability to quantify the extent of PFAS destruction versus transformation.

pfas_scope.value: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in general, including perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAA)
Newly detected PFAS classes: FASHN and MeOH-FASA
Transformation products and related PFAS structures: H-PFSA, PFPrES in the PFESA class, Me-FASASi, FASASA, Me-FASAA, Et-FASAA, N-SPAmP-FHxSA, N-SPAmP-FHxSAA, N-SPAmP-FHxSAPS, Bistriflimide
Other halogenated substances, including chlorinated and brominated compounds formed during EO treatment

residuals_byproducts.statement: Two new classes of PFAS (FASHN and MeOH-FASA) were discovered, including FASHN as a transformation-product class likely formed via substitution reactions involving hyponitrous acid generated from nitrate/nitrate radical chemistry during EO.

Detection of H-PFSA during EO treatment suggested a new pathway for its formation; additional PFAS-related transformation products (e.g., PFPrES in the PFESA class, various sulfonamide/sulfonate-related compounds such as Me-FASASi, FASASA, Me-FASAA, Et-FASAA, N-SPAmP-FHxSA, N-SPAmP-FHxSAA, N-SPAmP-FHxSAPS, and Bistriflimide) were also observed.

Six chlorinated or brominated compounds formed during EO treatment were detected, and foam fractionation pre-treatment appeared to influence their formation and/or degradation, indicating that advanced oxidation can generate non-fluorinated halogenated byproducts.

Ammonia present in the matrices was oxidized during EO, leading to nitrate and possibly nitrate-radical formation, which may contribute to formation of nitrogen-containing PFAS transformation products and other halogenated nitrogenous byproducts that can be more toxic than non-nitrogenous analogues.

Previous bioassays (cited by the authors) suggested that transformation products formed during EO had negligible biological activity compared with original pollutants, but the current study’s identification of potentially toxic transformation products underscores the need to monitor these residuals.

field_assessments.reason: The paper focuses on suspect and non-target screening to identify PFAS and other halogenated transformation products during EO of landfill leachate and groundwater, and explicitly highlights identification of new compounds and pathways rather than quantitative destruction metrics. No fluoride, fluorine mass balance, or mineralization measurements are reported in the cited text, so classifying comparability as descriptive_only is supported.

Cited sections describe EO as a destructive treatment and emphasize suspect/non-target screening to explore chemical space and transformation products, while noting knowledge gaps in untargeted analyses and toxicity/concentration of transformation products. They do not present quantitative removal efficiencies, defluorination extents, or mass balances, so the stated reason accurately reflects the study’s scope.

The abstract and introduction explicitly state that transformation products were identified, new pathways for PFAS transformation were found, and that suspect/non-target screening was used to explore transformation products (e.g., S16-E01, E02, E04, E05). Classifying this endpoint as transformation is consistent with the measured/identified outputs.

The interpretation that the study focused on identifying PFAS and other halogenated transformation products, including new classes, and that this highlights risks of incomplete destruction is directly supported by statements about identification of transformation products, new pathways, and the risk of incomplete degradation leading to transformation products (S16-E01, E04, E05, E07, E08).

The cited text notes that a previous study showed EO with boron-doped diamond anodes can successfully degrade PFAS (S16-E02) and that decreasing concentrations of several PFAS-related compounds during EO indicate they were transformed or mineralized (S16-E08). Using loss of parent (or specific PFAS-like) compounds as an endpoint is consistent with parent_compound_loss.

The interpretation that EO is capable of degrading PFAS and that this study mainly infers loss from decreasing concentrations of certain features is consistent with S16-E02 (successful degradation of PFAS with EO in previous work) and S16-E08 (decreasing concentrations of listed PFAS-like compounds interpreted as change into transformation products or mineralization). The text does not present detailed mass balances, aligning with the qualitative framing in the interpretation.

Defluorination is discussed conceptually (EO is assumed to unzip the perfluoroalkyl chain to achieve full defluorination; S16-E05), but there are no measurements of inorganic fluoride, total fluorine, or fluorine mass balance in the cited text. Since endpoint_type must reflect measured bases rather than conceptual goals, classifying this as a defluorination endpoint is not supported.

The interpretation explicitly states that defluorination and mineralization are discussed as desired outcomes and that this study does not report direct defluorination measurements. This matches S16-E05, which describes the assumed mechanism (unzip, full defluorination, complete mineralization) but also notes a focus on transformation products and need for untargeted analyses, not measurements of released fluoride.

Toxicity change is not measured in this study. The cited text (S16-E06, E07) refers to previous bioassays that showed ~90% reduction in activity and notes that transformation products identified here are unlikely to be significantly biologically active, but these are results from earlier work, not new assays in the present study. Endpoint_type should reflect measurements made in this work, so classifying toxicity_change as an endpoint of this study is not supported.

The interpretation correctly describes that previous bioassays (from an earlier study) showed large reductions in bioassay activity and that this work only cites those findings without conducting new toxicity tests (S16-E06, E07). This matches the cited text’s framing.

The endpoint is categorized as "other" to capture that EO is framed as a destructive treatment while the study’s main contribution is analytical (suspect and non-target screening). S16-E01 and E03–E05 describe EO as a destructive treatment and focus on identification of new compounds, making "other" an appropriate non-specific endpoint classification.

The interpretation that the study primarily provides analytical mapping of transformation products within a destructive-treatment context is consistent with S16-E01, E03–E05, and E07, which emphasize suspect/non-target screening, discovery of new PFAS classes, and monitoring transformation products, rather than quantifying destruction performance.

S16-E04 notes risk of formation of transformation products during EO and states that more studies are needed to determine their concentrations and toxicity. S16-E06 highlights risks of unknown transformation products potentially emitted to air. Together these support the author-reported limitation as written.

S16-E05 states that transformation products have not been widely investigated because most studies rely on targeted quantification of PFAS using triple-quadrupole MS and that there is an urgent need for untargeted analyses. This matches the described author-reported limitation and motivation.

S16-E07 explicitly states that the water matrix plays an important role in the types of chemicals that can be formed during EO. However, the added claim that this "complicates generalization of results" is an extrapolation not directly stated in the cited text. The core point (matrix-specific effects) is supported, but the generalization limitation is inferred rather than author-stated.

The cited sections (S16-E01, E02, E04, E05, E08) frame the study as using suspect and non-target screening to explore transformation products and knowledge gaps, without presenting fluorine or carbon mass balances or direct mineralization data. From the design, it necessarily follows that the extent of destruction versus transformation cannot be quantified, so this design_inferred limitation is supported.

The title and abstract (S16-E01) and other sections (e.g., S16-E02, E03, E04, E05, E07) repeatedly state that landfill leachate and groundwater were treated via EO, and S16-E03 describes foam fractionation as a pre-concentration step in some configurations. Describing the matrices as landfill leachate and groundwater, sometimes after foam fractionation, is accurate.

S16-E02 mentions EO with boron-doped diamond anodes, and S16-E05 notes anodic materials with high overpotential for the oxygen evolution reaction. Together they support the value "Boron-doped diamond with high overpotential for oxygen evolution" as the anode material description.
The operating condition is a descriptive material type rather than a numeric quantity; leaving the unit null is appropriate and consistent with the text.

S16-E03 explains foam fractionation as a concentration step relying on PFAS surfactant properties to create a PFAS-rich foam that can then be treated with EO (S16-E04). This supports the value that foam fractionation was used as a PFAS concentration step prior to EO in some experiments.
The qualifiers paraphrase S16-E03, which describes how foam fractionation uses PFAS surfactant properties and foam enrichment to concentrate PFAS prior to removal of the PFAS-rich foam fraction.
This operating condition is a process description rather than a numeric parameter, so a null unit is appropriate.

S16-E04 and E08 indicate that the matrices are landfill leachate and groundwater and note oxidation of ammonia and the presence of other halogenated/nitrogenous compounds. Describing them as complex matrices containing co-contaminants like ammonia and other halogenated and nitrogenous compounds is consistent with the cited text.

S16-E04 states that ammonia is oxidized during EO and that nitrate and nitrate radicals might contribute to formation of N-containing transformation products; S16-E08 documents an increase in nitrate from ammonia oxidation. The qualifier correctly summarizes this behavior.
This condition describes qualitative matrix characteristics and reaction pathways, so it appropriately has no unit.

The title and abstract (S16-E01) name per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) as the focus, and S16-E03 mentions perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAA) in the context of foam fractionation. The scope description of PFAS in general, including PFAA, is accurate.
S16-E04 clearly states that two new classes of PFAS, FASHN and MeOH-FASA, were discovered for the first time. This directly supports the field value.

S16-E08 lists the transformation products and related PFAS structures: H-PFSA, PFPrES in the PFESA class, Me-FASASi, FASASA, Me-FASAA, Et-FASAA, N-SPAmP-FHxSA, N-SPAmP-FHxSAA, N-SPAmP-FHxSAPS, and Bistriflimide. The record reproduces this scope accurately.

S16-E01 (abstract) and S16-E04 refer to "other halogenated compounds" and specifically to six chlorinated or brominated compounds formed during EO treatment. The value describing the inclusion of other halogenated substances, including chlorinated and brominated compounds formed during EO, is supported.

S16-E04 states that two new classes of PFAS (FASHN and MeOH-FASA) were discovered, that FASHN includes transformation products, and that these were possibly formed through a substitution reaction involving a hyponitrous acid functional group. This matches the described statement.

S16-E04 notes detection of H-PFSA and a potential new pathway for its formation during EO, and S16-E08 lists PFPrES in the PFESA class and multiple sulfonamide/sulfonate-related PFAS compounds, including those named in the field. The statement aligns with these descriptions.

S16-E04 reports detection of six chlorinated or brominated compounds formed during EO and that foam fractionation pre-treatment seemed to affect their formation and/or degradation. The inference that this indicates advanced oxidation can generate non-fluorinated halogenated byproducts follows directly from these findings and is not contradicted.

S16-E04 states that ammonia is oxidized during EO and that formation of nitrate and nitrate radicals might contribute to N-containing transformation products; it also notes literature findings that halogenated nitrogenous disinfection byproducts are more toxic than non-nitrogenous analogues. S16-E08 documents increased nitrate from ammonia oxidation. The statement accurately reflects these points.

S16-E06 and E07 mention previous bioassays that indicated transformation products were unlikely to be significantly biologically active compared to original pollutants, but also that potentially toxic transformation products formed during EO can be environmental hazards and that monitoring them is important. This supports the summarized statement.

Across S16-E01–E05, the text describes EO treatment of landfill leachate and groundwater using boron-doped diamond anodes, sometimes following foam fractionation. The scale description accurately reflects these experimental features.

S16-E01 and E03–E05 identify electrochemical oxidation with boron-doped diamond anodes as a destructive treatment for PFAS in landfill leachate and groundwater, with foam fractionation as a pre-concentration step in some cases. The treatment description matches this.

verification.record_usable_rationale: Core elements—source identity, matrix, treatment description, PFAS scope, and the qualitative focus on transformation products and non-target screening—are correctly supported by the cited text. Misclassifications involve two endpoints (defluorination and toxicity_change) that are discussed conceptually or via prior work rather than measured in this study; these are flagged as endpoint_classification issues but are clearly described in the record as not directly measured, so they do not fundamentally misrepresent the study’s destruction-performance evidence. Thus the record remains usable for synthesis with attention to the endpoint assessments provided.

comparability.reason: Aquarden experiment uses the same general matrix (PFOS-based AFFF), similar dilution factor (100×), continuous-flow SCWO, and targeted PFAS analytical approach as the Battelle and 374Water demonstrations, making destruction and defluorination endpoints broadly comparable when accounting for different system designs and lack of full product characterization.

endpoints.interpretation: Decrease in targeted parent PFOA concentration between AFFF influent and SCWO effluent was measured and interpreted by authors as evidence of PFAS destruction.

Inorganic fluoride concentration increased substantially in the effluent, while organic-fluorine bound in 28 targeted PFAS decreased, indicating conversion of organofluorine to fluoride (defluorination). Authors refer to this as fluorine mineralization.

Large reduction in COD and targeted PFAS was interpreted as significant oxidation and destruction of organic compounds in the AFFF, including PFAS, but without full closure of a fluorine or carbon balance.

Stoichiometric mass balance comparing fluorine in targeted PFAS versus measured fluoride in effluent indicated that targeted PFAS accounted for only 27% of measured fluoride, implying a large fraction of PFAS or other organofluorine compounds not captured by targeted analysis.

limitations.statement: Only 28 PFAS were quantified in the fluorine mass balance even though AFFF likely contains dozens of additional PFAS and other organofluorine compounds, so targeted analysis underestimates total organofluorine and limits interpretation of destruction.
No total organofluorine, TOP assay, or non-targeted screening data were collected, limiting the ability to fully characterize PFAS transformation products and unaccounted fluorine.
The demonstrations were time-limited, so long-term reactor performance and byproduct formation under continuous operation could not be assessed.
SCWO stepwise destruction may form small volatile organofluorine byproducts and smaller perfluorocarboxylic acids, but these were not comprehensively measured in this study.
